body.text: Most operas are known as the work of their composers, with the librettist quietly acknowledged, if at all, in the program. We might be aware of Mozart’s collaborations with Lorenzo Da Ponte or Richard Strauss’s with Hugo von Hofmannsthal, but an opera belongs to its composer.

The poet Gwen Harwood shared this view as she began writing librettos for Larry Sitsky’s operas in the 1960s. When she sent her words to Sitsky, she affirmed they were now his: “You own the librettos, not me!” She nevertheless drew the line at anyone besides Sitsky fiddling with her work, and was put out when she wasn’t offered tickets to the operas’ premieres. She was proud of her writing and ambivalent about her subservient role — as she was in her role as housewife and mother.

This collaboration came about after Rex Hobcroft, head of the Hobart Conservatorium of Music, organised a New Music festival in 1963. Though Harwood had aspired to becoming a concert pianist, by this time she was the mother of four children and notorious as the Hobart poet-housewife who had hoaxed the Bulletin with rude acrostic poems. Ann-Marie Priest’s 2022 biography of Harwood, My Tongue is My Own, reveals that she found Hobcroft’s performances of Beethoven’s piano concertos consoling to her sense of isolation and neglect.

At the New Music festival, she was so excited by Sitsky’s experimental compositions she wrote the poem “New Music” celebrating its creation of “a world out of unmeasured darkness/ pierced by a brilliant nerve of sound.” She began to feel her very facility with traditional form, rhyme and metre might be restricting her horizons as an artist.

Priest has now collected Harwood and Sitsky’s substantial thirty-year correspondence to reveal the nature of their opera collaborations and the possibilities for new musical creation during this interesting time for Australian culture. Three other collections of letters by Harwood have been published — she was a prolific and brilliant letter writer — but this is the only one offering both sides of the correspondence.

Though Hobcroft is not a correspondent in this collection, he is a significant third party in Harwood and Sitsky’s friendship, having first recommended Harwood to the composer as a potential librettist. Harwood regularly reports to Sitsky about Hobcroft and his family’s visits to her home and asks Sitsky about his well-being after he leaves Hobart. Hobcroft’s work promoting music in Hobart clearly had a profound effect on Harwood. It’s clear, too, that the ABC played a crucial role in keeping provincial Australians in touch with classical and experimental music.

Harwood and Sitsky began work on a one-act version of Edgar Allan Poe’s The Fall of the House of Usher, performed in 1965 at Hobart’s Theatre Royal alongside Margaret Sutherland’s The Young Kabbarli, an opera about Daisy Bates with a libretto by Maie Casey, wife of the then governor-general. Harwood, who had to buy her own ticket to the opening, was ready to mock the Australiana of which The Young Kabbarli was an expression, with its tendency to overblown expression of local colour. She and Sitsky were drawn to gloomier literary inspiration, including Kafka’s The Trial or the legend of the Jewish Golem.

Priest organises the letters according to each of the operas they worked on together, providing helpful summaries of the development of each idea and its progression to performance — or abandonment. She makes order out of a process that might appear untidy and random, the creators flailing around searching for suitable subjects then batting questions back and forth as the work develops. They find, for example, that The Trial is still in copyright and any thought of an opera must be abandoned. Sometimes Sitsky has several compositions on the go at once, and the possibilities for performance bring deadlines and shifts in concentration.

Sitsky composed to fit Harwood’s words, his atonal music following the pattern of the voices. Their method was to discuss potential ideas before deciding on a subject for Harwood to research and draft a libretto. Sitsky would then see what musical possibilities he could bring to it, often cutting words to fit musical phrasing or scenes to meet the demands of production. In the case of the radio opera Voices in Limbo, Harwood’s frustration becomes clear as she tries to invent a script for disembodied voices that allows the composer full scope for emotional effects.

Opera composing may seem a serious occupation, but Harwood adopts a breezy attitude to the task. When she read Georg Büchner’s novel about Goethe’s depressive friend Jacob Lenz she declared, “Lenz is beaut, it won’t take me long to whip up something.” And it does seem she found the task relatively easy. In 1974 the resulting one-act opera was chosen to try out the new Sydney Opera House stage alongside Felix Werder’s The Affair, and it received much critical acclaim. Harwood later saw it as her greatest achievement but didn’t publish it separately as it “rightly belongs to Larry.”

Sitsky never seems to run out of ideas for new compositions, nor is he daunted by the task of getting his operas onstage. He continues to write new works for piano and perform concerts around the country, and sometimes overseas, while teaching at the Canberra School of Music. At times during the period covered by these letters, those performances become burdensome, dragging him away from his creative work to spend long hours practising piano. At one point he declares, “I hate the piano.”

His hard work applying for support and negotiating with potential producers meant the pair had a remarkable run of success in getting their operas into performance. Lenz, Fiery Tales (based on a mix of Boccaccio and Chaucer’s “Miller’s Tale”) and The Golem gained main-stage productions and good reviews, and De Profundis (a setting of Wilde’s letter from Reading Gaol) was performed in several concert versions.

The letters in the section titled “The Dreaded Bicentennial” are both amusing and revealing of the opposing pressures of nationalism at the time. Neither librettist nor composer can muster enthusiasm for what Harwood called the “mishmash of Aboriginal legends, explorers, drovers’ wives, wholemeal bread, love, joy, motherhood etc. etc” commissioned from them by the Bicentennial Authority. They gave up, and Harwood returned her fee to the School of Music.

It is surprising to find that a creative collaboration could endure over such a distance with few in-person consultations or lengthy phone calls, let alone email and zoom. Until quite late in the partnership, with interstate phone calls prohibitively expensive, mail was their prime means of communication. Sitsky visited Hobart once or twice a year, but the letters are a near-complete record of their work together.

They also detail the ephemera of domestic life as the two families deal with moving house, illnesses, miscarriage and births, and bushfires. They are enlivened by Harwood’s cheeky verses and wry comments, including a hilarious account of a poetry reading in Sydney in 1970 where Tom Shapcott broke the boredom by launching into an orgasm poem molto appassionato. The Fraser government comes in for criticism for its stinginess in funding the creative arts.

But these are essentially letters about work. At times, Sitsky is so busy juggling his various commitments that his wife, Magda, writes letters for him, usually with more detail and news. Harwood may seem to take her writing in her stride but she admits that she is “so used to working in short periods of time snatched between one task & the next that I feel poetically like a short-order cook: if only they would lock me up with the drink and a dictionary I would churn out epics.” Sitsky knows he’s a workaholic, telling Harwood: “Am working very hard at relaxing.”

Adding further to the pressures, Harwood takes on physical labour as well as her creative work, especially when she and her husband Bill move to a rural plot at Oyster Cove. There, they keep animals, build dams and manage in fairly primitive conditions, with Harwood the only driver for the necessary trips to town. As in so much of her life, she seems to choose difficulty over comfort.

Harwood’s final illness ended the plans for an opera based on Henry Handel Richardson’s Maurice Guest, the kind of naturalist novel that inspired so many classic operas and would have given an Australian slant to European tragedy.

These letters leave us knowing everything about these compositions except the works themselves. Priest does her best to give us a sense of how they worked in performance with summaries of the reviews. The pattern for Australian operas, though, is for one brief season of performance before being consigned to oblivion. This, after an immense struggle to production. A recording of Lenz is available from ABC Classics and Lyall Bevan’s performance of De Profundis is currently available on Apple Music. The success rate of new operas is, of course, always low, and it is difficult to imagine any company committing itself to restaging the three hours of The Golem.

Writing to Sitsky in her final months, Harwood recalled the opening night of The Golem as a high point of her life: “it’s enough for me to have stood onstage holding the Golem’s muddy hand and your creative hand on that glorious night.” •
